groups.title: Exchange rates
groups.explainer: Charities do different kinds of good: raising incomes, adding years of healthy life, sparing animals pain, making people more satisfied with their lives. To rank them on one list, results are shown in years of healthy life, and the rates below say what the other kinds of good are worth against each other. Animal analyses are first put into days of a chicken's pain, each species weighed against a chicken. Change them and the ranking changes; that is the point.

groups.title: Lives
groups.explainer: How much saving a life counts. A value judgment, not a fact.

groups.title: Lives near and far
groups.explainer: Whether a life counts the same wherever it is. By default it does, and nothing here changes any figure. Some people give more weight to people (and animals) nearer to them: set where you live and how much less each step further away counts, and every estimate is weighed by where the lives it helps are.

groups.title: Timing
groups.explainer: How much less good done in the future counts than the same good done today, and how much less an old estimate counts than a new one.

groups.title: How impact is counted
groups.explainer: How credit for an outcome is shared between everyone who paid for it, for how long a won reform counts, and how much the next dollar does compared with an organisation's past average, and how much a programme counts whose results aren't measured.

rows.label: Credit by share of resources
rows.technical: Pro-rata attribution instead of counterfactual credit
rows.explainer:
Off: each evaluator's counterfactual logic, as published, such as GiveWell's adjustments for money a grant pulls in or pushes elsewhere.

On: an outcome is shared out by everything that went into it: every funder's money, governments' in-kind costs, and staff's pay below what they could earn elsewhere. Each gets the share it paid for, so shares add up to 100% and nothing is counted twice.

Where we don't know a charity's staff costs or pay, we use a default for its kind of work: low for programs that hand out nets or medicines, high for research and advocacy.

rows.label: Years a won reform counts before it would have come anyway
rows.technical: Years of a corporate commitment's or policy's effect credited to the campaign that won it (years brought forward)
rows.explainer:
When a campaign wins a reform (a company's cage-free pledge, a ban on low-welfare imports, a climate rule), the change would probably have come some day anyway: other campaigners, the market or the law would have got there. The campaign gets credit only for the years it brought the change forward. This sets how many years that is, for every model that credits a won reform.

Evaluators answer it very differently for the same kind of win: Founders Pledge credits The Humane League 0.5 to 1.5 years per policy, Animal Charity Evaluators 3.9 to 20.5 years (and Rethink Priorities' 15 for cage-free pledges), Ambitious Impact counts 35 to 55 years. The default, 5, is about the middle of the evaluators' own figures; the range, 1 to 20, covers nearly all of them. Our judgment.

The years are counted from when the reform takes effect (a pledge's deadline, a law's start) and, like every future benefit, discounted at "Next year's good counts less by", the wait included. Each evaluator's own figure is shown on its model as the evaluator's, and used in the evaluator view.

rows.label: How much the next dollar does compared with the average dollar so far
rows.technical: A marginal dollar's result as a share of the organisation's past average result (marginal ÷ average cost-effectiveness)
rows.explainer:
Some estimates divide what an organisation spent in the past by everything that spending achieved: the pledges, laws and research results it won, the lives its service saved, or the money it moved. That is the average dollar. A dollar given now does less, because an organisation does its most promising work first and the easiest wins are taken. This sets how much the next dollar does, as a share of the average, for every model built that way: The Life You Can Save's money moved, the climate models built on past budgets and past wins, Animal Charity Evaluators' and Founders Pledge's campaign estimates, Founders Pledge's Innovation in Government Initiative, and SoGive's research and lifeboat estimates. Estimates that are already about the next dollar (GiveWell's, Ambitious Impact's and the Happier Lives Institute's, forward-looking budgets) and costs per item delivered (a net, a treatment, a course, a tree) don't take it, so nothing is counted twice; docs/normalization.md lists every model.

The few published comparisons: CEARCH puts Giving What We Can's marginal giving multiplier at about 13× against its 2020–22 average of 30× (0.43), and in another reading at 17.6% of the average; Giving What We Can expects its marginal figure to be much closer to the average (up to 1). Rethink Priorities' funding model assumes each doubling of a fund's budget cuts its cost-effectiveness by about 10% for GiveWell and 46% for a catastrophic-risk fund, which puts the next dollar at 85% and 11% of the average. Open Philanthropy treats returns to funding as roughly logarithmic, under which an organisation that has grown its spending tenfold does about 40% as much with its next dollar as with its average one. The default, 50%, is our judgment; the range, 18% to 100% (the next dollar as good as the average), covers these figures.

The evaluator's view keeps 100%: the evaluators publish the average.

rows.label: How much we count a programme whose results aren't measured
rows.technical: Discount on every branch of a model whose outcome isn't measured for this charity (its reach or effect rests on the research literature or on judgment), the same everywhere: the row missing_data_adj (docs/normalization.md 2.12)
rows.explainer:
Every programme of every charity is counted, even one that publishes little or nothing about what it achieved. Where a charity doesn't measure a programme's results, we build its estimate from the research on that kind of work (meta-analyses and trials of the intervention: how much it does per person or per dollar, and for how long), applied to the programme's own spending and whatever reach it reports, with wide ranges; we never borrow another charity's result. The same goes for any part of a model whose reach or effect is our judgment rather than the charity's own data. A programme that doesn't measure its results is probably not the typical one in the research: programmes that measure tend to be the ones that work, and the literature carries none of this programme's own detail. So every such estimate counts less, by this share, the same way in every model.

A part of a model counts in full only when the charity's own count of who got the intervention meets an effect measured with a credible comparison: its own controlled evaluation, or trials of the same intervention delivered the same way (doses delivered and a trial's effect, for example). The default, 50%, is our judgment; the range runs from 10% (an unmeasured programme does little next to measured ones) to 100% (it does as well as the research says).

rows.label: Healthy year vs doubled-income year
rows.technical: Units of value per DALY (disability-adjusted life year) averted
rows.explainer:
A doubled-income year is one person's income doubled for one year, the measure GiveWell uses. This says how many of those a year of healthy life is worth.

Our rough default: GiveWell values saving a young child at about 116 doubled-income years, and that adds about 60 years of life, so about 2 each. The 1–4 range is ours.

rows.label: Healthy hours lost per day of disabling pain
rows.explainer:
Animal models count days of disabling pain, with milder pain as a fraction of a day, in chickens; the chicken slider says what a chicken's day is worth in a person's. This says how much healthy life a person's day of disabling pain costs: about 10 hours by default, 2 to 24 in the range.

Nobody publishes this rate, so it's the least grounded number on the site, and it often decides whether animal charities rank above global health.

rows.label: 1 point more life satisfaction for a year vs a year of healthy life
rows.technical: Healthy years (DALYs averted) per WELLBY (wellbeing-adjusted life year)

source.title: Calibrated on depression: GBD 2019 disability weights on the PHQ-9 (facts: depression.dalys_per_phq9_point_year, depression.phq9_sd) and HLI's 2 WELLBYs per standard-deviation-year (facts: wellby_factors.wellbys_per_sd_year)
source.note: Default = PHQ-9 SD 4.2117 × 0.031 healthy years per point-year ÷ 2 WELLBYs per SD-year = 0.0652815 healthy years per WELLBY (src/engine/wellby-calibration.test.ts keeps it in step with the facts). Stated in healthy years, so the calibration holds whatever "Healthy year vs doubled-income year" is set to.

rows.explainer:
The Happier Lives Institute counts good in life satisfaction (0–10) for a year, its WELLBY, and doesn't convert it to health or income. This says what one such point is worth in healthy years, so its analyses can be ranked with the rest.

The default makes depression count the same whichever way it is measured. Most of HLI's analyses are of therapy for depression, and the site counts a fall in depression as health: the Global Burden of Disease weights for mild, moderate and severe depression on the PHQ-9 questionnaire, 0.031 healthy years per point for a year, which Founders Pledge's and SoGive's StrongMinds analyses also go through. One standard deviation of depression for a year is about 4.2 PHQ-9 points, so 0.13 healthy years; HLI counts it as 2 WELLBYs. So a WELLBY is worth 0.065 healthy years. Because the rate is in healthy years, the two routes agree whatever "Healthy year vs doubled-income year" is set to: WELLBY models, like DALY models, don't move with that slider. Every HLI model, depression or not, converts at this rate; deaths in HLI models are valued the site's way and don't move with it.

Other views: HLI's own 2021 moral-weights work implies about 0.275 (0.55 doubled-income years at 2 a healthy year); matching GiveDirectly's cash transfers, the one programme HLI and GiveWell both measured (HLI 7.55 WELLBYs per $1,000, GiveWell's Kenya estimate 4.36 healthy years per $1,000), gives 0.575, which is where HLI's own results sit relative to cash. At 0.575 HLI's therapy charities count about 9 times more than at the default, and Founders Pledge's and SoGive's analyses of the same therapy don't move. The evaluator view converts HLI's models at 0.575, so they keep their place relative to GiveDirectly as HLI sees it.

rows.label: A chicken's suffering vs a person's
rows.technical: Chicken's welfare range relative to a person's
rows.explainer:
How much a chicken's suffering counts next to the same suffering in a person. The default, 33%, is Rethink Priorities' median welfare range for chickens; their 90% range is 0.2% to 87%. In an informal survey, most people answered about 0.2% (500 chickens to one person).

Every animal model counts its result in chicken-equivalent pain days: each species weighed against a chicken by Rethink Priorities' estimates, with Ambitious Impact's own species weights taken out of ACE's figures first. So this one value sets how all animals compare with people.

Set it to 0 if a chicken's suffering shouldn't count; raise it, up to 100%, if it counts as much as a person's.

rows.label: Weigh each species by Rethink Priorities' estimates
rows.technical: Rethink Priorities' welfare ranges instead of Ambitious Impact's species weights
rows.explainer: On (our view): each species counts by Rethink Priorities' welfare range relative to a chicken (facts/welfare_ranges.json). Off (the evaluator view): by the species weights inside Ambitious Impact's suffering-adjusted days, so ACE's own results reproduce. Not offered as a control: the chicken slider is the one animal weight readers set.

rows.label: Value of doubling an income for a year
rows.technical: Units of value per unit of ln(consumption)
rows.explainer: GiveWell's weight on income gains, kept fixed: it defines a doubled-income year, the measure the other exchange rates are set in. Moving it would do the same as moving all of them together.

rows.label: Deaths caused by one more tonne of CO₂
rows.technical: Mortality cost of carbon: deaths per tonne of CO₂e, from heat and fossil-fuel air pollution

source.title: Rethink Priorities, Cross-cause cost-effectiveness: climate change versus global health (Clare & Vargas, 2026)

rows.explainer:
Climate charities count the tonnes of CO₂ (and other greenhouse gases, as CO₂-equivalents) they keep out of the air. To compare them with everything else, we ask how many deaths one more tonne causes, and value each death like any other adult's death on the site.

The default, 1.9 deaths per 10,000 tonnes, is Rethink Priorities' estimate (facts: climate.deaths_per_tco2e): 0.43 from heat and 1.46 from the fine-particle air pollution that comes with burning fossil fuels. Rethink counts the heat deaths until 2300 without discounting; we discount them at "Next year's good counts less by" over the years until they come ("Years until the heat deaths from a tonne of CO₂", 60 by default), as every model discounts future good. Air-pollution deaths come the same year and aren't discounted. The range runs from heat alone (0.43) to the tops of Rethink's intervals (5.1), which is also about what Rethink's estimate of all climate damage, crops and sea level included, comes to in lives.

Each death is valued by the age it happens at, like every other death on the site: GiveWell's moral weights by age (facts: moral_weights) over the ages of today's heat deaths (60 doubled-income years on average) and air-pollution deaths (48: nine in ten are of people over 50; facts: death_ages, GBD 2023), times "A child's life vs doubled-income year", so climate moves with the same weight on lives as health charities. At the defaults a tonne kept out of the air some other way than burning less fuel (a forest, a methane leak) cuts only the discounted heat deaths, about 1 hour of healthy life (a charity that cuts one for $1 does about 0.12 years of healthy life per $1,000); a tonne from burning less fossil fuel, with the world-average smoke behind Rethink's figure, is worth about 1.3 days (3.6 years per $1,000 at $1 a tonne). Most tonnes sit in between: coal smoke per tonne is far above gas's, and a US plant with scrubbers far below the world average.

For comparison, the US government's social cost of carbon of $185 a tonne (Rennert et al. 2022) rests on the same heat-death count but values deaths in poor countries and in the future less; Giving What We Can's 2016 estimate is about 50 times lower than our default, mainly because it leaves out air pollution. Climate damage that isn't deaths (lost crops, income, migration) and tail risks are not counted: our judgment, stated as a fact set to 0 (climate.nondeath_damages_vs_deaths) so it shows, and the reason the default is likely low. Tonnes that come without fuel smoke (a forest left standing, a methane leak stopped) count only for their heat deaths; each climate model has its own row for how much air pollution its tonnes cut, relative to an average fossil-fuel tonne, from the share of its tonnes that come from burning less fuel and the smoke that fuel makes.

rows.label: A child's life vs doubled-income year
rows.technical: Life value multiplier on GiveWell's moral weights
rows.explainer: How many doubled-income years saving a young child's life is worth. GiveWell uses about 116, from donor surveys, a survey in Ghana and Kenya, and staff judgment; this scales its weights for every age. The 70–163 range is ours.

rows.label: Where you live
rows.technical: Home country (ISO 3166 numeric code; 0 = not set)
rows.explainer: The country the distance weight counts from. Not set (the default) means no distance weighting at all: every life counts the same wherever it is. Countries are grouped into world regions by the UN's standard list (M49: Northern America, Western Europe, Eastern Africa and so on; facts/countries.json).

rows.label: Each step further from you, a life counts less by
rows.technical: Discount per step of distance: your country, the rest of your world region, the rest of the world
rows.explainer: A value judgment, not a fact. With a country set under Where you live, a life (a person's or an animal's) in your own country counts in full, one elsewhere in your world region counts less by this much, and one in the rest of the world by this much again: at 50%, a life in your country counts 1, one in your region 0.5 and one further away 0.25. Each estimate is weighed by where the lives it helps are (each model's beneficiaries: the countries its programme works in, or the whole world by population for climate and research with global reach); a charity that moves money takes each destination's weight. 0% (the default) counts every life the same, which is what every evaluator on the site does; the evaluator's own view never applies it.

rows.label: Next year's good counts less by
rows.explainer: How much less good done a year from now counts, compounding each year. GiveWell uses 4%; ACE uses 4% in some reviews and 1.4% in others. It moves only models that discount explicitly, such as ACE's cage-free and shrimp campaigns and the long-term income gains in GiveWell's bed net and seasonal malaria models; GiveDirectly's and Helen Keller's have 4% built in. It also discounts the heat deaths a tonne of CO₂ causes decades from now ("Years until the heat deaths from a tonne of CO₂"). It is also how much future generations count: a catastrophe that costs the future loses every later year of healthy life, each discounted at this rate, so the loss is the yearly loss ÷ the rate (25 years' worth at 4%, 1,000 at the lowest setting, 0.1%: the slider stops there because at 0 an endless future would count infinitely).

rows.label: Each year since an estimate was made, it counts less by
rows.technical: Annual discount on a cost-effectiveness estimate's age
rows.explainer: How much less to trust a cost-effectiveness estimate for each year since its evaluator published it, compounding like the discount rate: at 5% a 2-year-old estimate counts 91% and a 10-year-old one 61%. Evaluators re-check what they recommend every year or two (GiveWell updates its top charities' models several times a year; Animal Charity Evaluators re-evaluates its recommended charities every two years, and Founders Pledge about every two years) and withdraw some recommendations, so an estimate nobody has renewed for years may no longer stand. The site's own data can't set the rate: GiveWell's successive estimates of the same programme (41 pairs, about a year apart) move a lot, typically two-thirds up or 40% down, but not mostly down (39% of them fell, and on average they rose a few percent a year). So 5% is a judgment, between 0% (what the revisions alone support) and 15%. An estimate's age counts from its publication date to the date the site's data was last refreshed (2 November 2026), so results don't change with the day you look. Every model on the rankings takes it; a charity that moves money takes it on its own estimate and on each destination's. The evaluator's own view never applies it.

rows.label: Years until the heat deaths from a tonne of CO₂
rows.technical: Discount-weighted delay between emitting a tonne of CO₂e and the extra heat deaths it causes

source.title: Clare & Vargas (2026), Rethink Priorities, quoting Bressler (2021), The mortality cost of carbon, Nature Communications
source.quote: These [deaths] are concentrated at the end of the century when global average temperatures are highest and marginal changes to temperatures are most damaging.

rows.explainer:
A tonne of CO₂ emitted now warms the planet for centuries, but the deaths that warming causes come late: both Bressler (2021) and Rennert et al. (2022), whose model Rethink Priorities re-ran, find them concentrated at the end of the century, when it is hottest and each extra bit of warming does most harm. Rethink counts them to 2300 without discounting. We discount them like any other future good, as if they all came this many years after the tonne: 60 by default (about 2085 for a tonne cut today), 30 to 100 in the range. Our judgment; no source gives the year-by-year profile. At 4% a year, a death 60 years away counts about a tenth of one today.

Air-pollution deaths are not delayed: fuel that isn't burned saves them the same year, so they aren't discounted.

rows.label: Share of a tonne's deaths that come from heat
rows.technical: Heat deaths ÷ (heat + air-pollution deaths) per tonne of CO₂e, Rethink Priorities' medians

source.title: Clare & Vargas (2026), Rethink Priorities (facts: climate.deaths_per_tco2e_heat and climate.deaths_per_tco2e_air_pollution)

rows.explainer: Of Rethink Priorities' 1.9 deaths per 10,000 tonnes, 0.43 come from heat and 1.46 from the fine particles that come with burning fossil fuels: heat is 23%. Fixed, not a slider: it splits whatever you set for "Deaths caused by one more tonne of CO₂" into deaths that come decades later (heat, discounted) and deaths that come at once (air pollution). Every tonne cuts the heat part; only tonnes that come from burning less fossil fuel near people cut the air-pollution part, and each climate model says how much of it its tonnes carry (its row "Air pollution these tonnes cut, relative to an average fossil-fuel tonne").

uov.label: GiveWell units of value
uov.explainer: One unit = doubling one person's consumption for one year.

sad.label: suffering-adjusted days averted
sad.explainer: Ambitious Impact's unit: days of an animal's pain, weighted by intensity and by Ambitious Impact's weight for the species, so one equals a day of a person's disabling pain. ACE reports in it; every animal model converts it into chicken-equivalent pain days before ranking. A model reporting SADs directly is converted as chickens' SADs, divided by Ambitious Impact's 2024 weight for a hen (0.463966, facts: aim_sads.chicken_2024).

ced.label: chicken-equivalent pain days averted
ced.explainer: Days of disabling pain spared, counted in chickens: each species' days times how much it can suffer relative to a chicken (Rethink Priorities). Converted to healthy years with how a chicken's suffering compares with a person's and the healthy hours a day of disabling pain costs.

wellby.label: wellbeing-adjusted life years
wellby.explainer: One point of life satisfaction (0–10) for one person for one year. Used by the Happier Lives Institute.

tco2e.label: tonnes of CO₂-equivalent averted
tco2e.explainer: Greenhouse gas kept out of the air, in tonnes of CO₂ or the same warming from other gases. Converted through the deaths one more tonne causes ("Deaths caused by one more tonne of CO₂"): every tonne avoids its heat deaths, discounted over the years until they come; a tonne that comes from burning less fossil fuel near people also avoids air-pollution deaths, at once. How much of that air pollution a model's tonnes carry is the model's own row "Air pollution these tonnes cut, relative to an average fossil-fuel tonne" (air_pollution_weight): 0 for a forest, a methane leak or CO₂ captured at a running plant; the share of tonnes from burning less fuel times how much smoke that fuel makes per tonne for the rest. A model whose evaluator counts air-pollution deaths directly (Founders Pledge's US coal-plant deaths for Clean Air Task Force) adds them per tonne in its row extra_deaths_per_tco2e (0 everywhere else). Each death is valued by the age it happens at, like every death on the site: GiveWell's moral weights by age (facts: moral_weights) over the ages of today's heat deaths and air-pollution deaths (facts: death_ages, GBD 2023), 59.7 and 47.6 units of value at the defaults, times the value-of-life slider. Damage that isn't death counts as nothing (facts: climate.nondeath_damages_vs_deaths, our judgment).

daly.label: DALYs averted
daly.explainer: Disability-adjusted life years averted. Converted into units of value with the shared DALY exchange rate.
